## Verifying R

- Test your IDE
  - Open your IDE
  - Start Session
  - Enter 2 + 2 in the console; verify the computing engine is working properly
- Test package installation
  - In the console type "install.packages("here")"
  - In the console type "library(here)"

## Verifying Paths

Loading and saving files and functions within a direcotry requires appropriate setting of path on your machine. The path tells the program where to look.

R Studio

- Best practice is to work within R Projects. The working directory becomes wherever the RProj file is located.
  - File -\> New Project -\> New or Existing Directory depending upon your use case -\> Quarto Project
  - For future work sessions, be sure to open the project, not just the files.
  - All files can then be loaded (or saved) relative to that working directory e.g. read.csv("./Data/fakedata.csv")
- You can also manually set the working directory via the gear icon in the Files panel or use setwd("C:/Users/Mike/Documents")

Positron

- Positron doesn't leverage RProjects (though they can be added)
- Instead, place a simple yaml file where you want the root working directory to be located.
  - File -\> New Text File
  - project: type: default
  - Save filename as \_quarto.yml
- Wherever you place that yml is the root working directory for this project, permitting you to use relative path referencing e.g. read.csv("./Data/fakedata.csv")

Task: 

- Set your working directory in your preferred IDE 
- Enter getwd() in the console to verify the working directory is where you intended

# Git

## Why need Version Control?

Don't do:

- first version.R
- first version_19J.R
- Final.R
- Final_v2.R
- Final_v2_last.R

Why? 

1.  Confusion over version ordering; "which is the final version?"
2.  Can't answer: "I need to revert back to the version that had my original approach. Which is that?""
3.  Poor naming convention is unprofessional delivery to clients

## Version Control Tools
A version control system includes proper naming convention and tools to track and manage changes.  

- Git: version control system
  - Tracks changes to files (not just code)
  - Stores the complete history of a project
  - Enables branching and merging
  - Works entirely on your local computer
- GitHub: cloud platform that lists Git repositories and supports collaboration
  - Stores copies of Git repositories online
  - Synchronizes work across multiple computers
  - Facilitates collaboration
  - Adds features beyond Git itself (pull requests, code review, GitHub Actions, Classroom, Organizations, etc.)
- GitHub Desktop: 
  - Local interface to GitHub

## Managing Conflicts
If you are working across multiple machines or with teammates, conflicts within the code may occur. 

A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot determine automatically how to combine two different versions of the same file.

This most often happens when:

two people edit the same lines of the same file,
you make local changes while someone else changes the GitHub version,
you pull changes from GitHub that overlap with your own uncommitted or committed work.

Git does not guess which version is correct. Instead, it stops the merge and asks you to decide what the final version of the file should contain.

The basic process is:

- Git attempts to combine the two versions.
- If the changes do not overlap, Git merges them automatically.
- If the changes conflict, Git marks the conflicting section.
- You edit the file and decide what to keep.
- You save the corrected file.
- You stage and commit the resolved version.

### Example

- Suppose the student has a file called Analysis.qmd. 
- The students is editing the file with the text: "We use stock prices from Yahoo Finance"
- But before the student pulls the latest version the instructor is editing the same line with "We use adjusted stock prices from Yahoo Finance"
- The student pulls the repo
- Git may produce a conflict. You will get a merge conflict warning along with the list of file(s) that are conflicted. 

R Studio

- After the failed pull, open the Git pane
- The conflicted fill will appear
- Its status should be unmerged of conflicted
- Click that file to open in the editor
- Inside the file Git will insert conflict markers such as: 
```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
We use daily stock prices from Yahoo Finance.
=======
We use adjusted daily stock prices from Yahoo Finance.
>>>>>>> origin/main
```
- The first block is your local version.  The second block is the version coming from GitHub
- To resolve the conflict, edit the file as you desire. 
- Remove all of the conflict markers: <<<, ====, >>>>>
- Save the file
- In the git pane, check the box next to the resolved file to Stage it
- Click commit
- Enter a commit message
- Commit the change
- Push the change

Positron

- Similar to the above, but somewhat more visual
- After the failed pull, open the source control panel
- Look under the Merge Changes or conflicted files
- Click the conflicted file
- Depending upon your version you shoudl see controls such as "accept current change", "accept incoming change", "accept both changes"
- You can also edit manually
- Once you are satisfied, save the file, return to source control, and stage the resolved file
- Enter a commit message
- Commit
- Push the change





## Version Control Best Practices

- Never commit sensitive information; e.g. don't put API keys in public repo
- Small commits are better than large commits; e.g.
  - Bad: Fix plot
  - Better: commit 1: fixed axes plotting bug; commit 2: auto-updated date in title, etc..
- Use descriptive commit messages:
  - Bad: update
  - Better: Engineered data for m/m % delta
- Data Storage
  - Git storage capacity is typically XXX.



# Project Design Best Practices

## Product Design

Think like a start-up founder

- Customer
- Problem
- Their current solution
- Your solution
- Why is your solution better?
- Wireframes

## Project Design Best Practices

- Whiteboard before keyboard
  - Always think and artchitect the project's methodology, coding structure, and goals before you start coding
- Folder Architecture
  - Always include README
  - Standard Repo's include: data, supporting, code, production
- Code Schematic
  - Visual guide of workflow
  - Think of your project as a machine. Map out how data enters the machine, how it is transformed, and how it is output.

# Coding Best Practices

## Housekeeping Best Practices

- Get into the habit of clearing memory and console at the top of every QMD
- Use a SetUp file to install and invoke packages and define any other global variables used throughout the project.
- Configuration for local files should be done near the top of the file within housekeeping; e.g. Define params as a list containing start_date, end_date, etc..

## Avoid Hard Coding Values

- E.g. you might need the starting date of your data repeatedly; during data acquisition, EDA, viz, etc…
- Best practice is to define a start_date object and use that throughout the code.
- Doing so permit easy code editing and facilitates object orientation; e.g. converting code to a function and looping

## Object Naming Conventions

- Use descriptive names whenever possible; e.g. returns_trainingset, not data
- Use standard name for temporary data objects; e.g. “temp”
- Don’t carry “temp” across chunks
- Delete temp before saving workspace

## Paths

- Absolute paths: “C:\Users\mda3\\MyDocument”
- Relative paths: “.\FDS-2026”
- Relative paths permit
  - Easy referencing of code and data files within the project
  - Transfer of project to a different machine
  - Situation to avoid: you ship your production code to your client, but your absolute path is mapping to your machine, and so they can’t run anything.

## Code Comments

- Professional grade code commentary should be motivated by someone having never seen your code and who is not code native being able to read and understand what’s happening.
- Every code chunk should have a description of it’s execution and purpose.
- Smaller code chunks generally lead to better commentary.
- Within a quarto environment you can chunk within the code block or within the qmd directly. The former is useful for research purposes, the later is useful for production.

## File Naming

- Myriad philosophies.
- I like to use filename_v1.qmd, filename_v2.qmd, etc..
- I commit and push changes to each version.
- I switch to the next version number to reflect major changes in the code.\
- I keep the “filename.qmd” as the final production version.
- If file dependencies are important (e.g. linking functions, etc..), then you can always have the most recent edition saved without version number.

## Data Handling

- Never overwrite your raw data
  - If you transform or append in local memory, then save as a new file
- Always save the "data" folder in the root directory for easy access
